title: Night people
hook: those who turn night into day are living backwards (Letters 122)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was surface shine: gold on the ceiling, and a soul nobody looks at. Your line was under the gold.

It's 1:40 in the morning. The phone is a small sun on your face. You meant to sleep an hour ago, and somehow you're watching a stranger restore a rusty knife. Letter 122 opens in autumn. The days are getting shorter, and Seneca says a good person still gets up early, as if to borrow back the light. Then he turns to a set of Romans who did the opposite on purpose: wealthy people who slept through the day, dined at midnight, went to bed at dawn, and thought it made them interesting.
screen: `1:40 AM, A STRANGER'S RUSTY KNIFE.` → `AUTUMN: THE DAYS GROW SHORT.` → `ROMANS WHO LIVED BY NIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, antipodes in the same city. Seneca borrows a joke from old Cato: there are people who have never once seen the sun rise or set. Seneca calls them antipodes, the people imagined living on the underside of the earth, except these live on the underside of the same street. Second, the neighbor you could tell time by. A storyteller named Pedo told Seneca about a man next door who lived entirely backwards. Pedo could tell the hour of the night by the sounds coming over the wall: the accounts being read, the singing practice, the carriage being readied, all while the rest of Rome slept. Third, why they did it. Not for work. It was a fashion. Doing what everyone else does felt cheap; reversing the clock got you noticed. Seneca calls it a vice that wants to be talked about. Living against nature, he says, is like wanting roses in winter or drinking on an empty stomach: the effort is the point. Fourth, a fair word for night workers. Seneca's target is the luxury of it, not the nurse on a night shift, the baker, the parent up with a baby. Those people aren't living backwards. They're carrying the night so others can sleep. His question is for the rest of us, awake at 1:40 for no reason we could name.
screen: `ANTIPODES ON THE SAME STREET.` · `PEDO TELLS TIME BY THE NOISE.` · `A VICE THAT WANTS TO BE TALKED ABOUT.` · `NOT THE NIGHT SHIFT: THE IDLE NIGHT.` · then, large: `WITH THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Look at tonight before it arrives, and name the hour that would give you enough sleep, and the thing most likely to steal it: the phone, a show, one more task. Picture yourself at that hour putting it down, in another room if you can, and lying in the dark with nothing left to prove. If your work keeps you up at night, picture your own rest instead, whatever hour it comes.
Night people. In Letter 122, Romans who slept by day and feasted by night to be noticed. Seneca calls it living backwards. Today's word.
Your line: with the sun. Even in autumn, a good day borrows back the light. Day four hundred eighty-eight, done.

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoic living keep a regular bedtime and an early start, treating the hours of light as the natural frame for their day, as Seneca urges in Letter 122.

fork.setup: you're a wealthy Roman. everyone dines at sunset. how do you get noticed, by Seneca's account?
options: sleep all day and dine at midnight.
fork.reveal: some did exactly that, and Seneca calls it a vice that wants to be talked about: living backwards.

original.note: Latin from Greek, 'opposite-footed': Seneca's name for Romans who lived by night.

what a scholar hears: 'antipodes' were a learned idea in Seneca's day, people imagined on the far side of a round earth; Seneca turns geography into a joke about neighbors.

chat.says: Was Seneca against everyone who's awake at night?
options: No; his target was people living backwards for show, not those working nights.
Yes; he said anyone awake after dark was living against nature, whatever the reason.
No; he admired night people for standing out from the boring crowd.
chat.meaning: Letter 122 mocks a fashion: Romans who reversed the clock to be noticed. A night-shift nurse or a parent with a baby isn't living backwards.

antipodes.meaning: people imagined living on the underside of the earth

Cato.meaning: an old Roman whose joke Seneca borrows

notes: Letters 122 paraphrased: the shortening days and rising early (122.1), 'antipodes in the same city' and Cato's line about never seeing sunrise or sunset (122.2), living against nature compared to roses in winter and drinking on an empty stomach (122.6–8), the vice that wants notice (122.14–18). Confirm section numbers and similes.

The neighbor in Pedo's story is Sextus Papinius (122.15–16); the script describes the noises generally (accounts, singing practice, carriage). Confirm the details and that the script's version doesn't overstate them.
